A community garden lives or dies on people, not plants, so the first month should be heavier on social work than on soil.

Week 1: Build the founding group. Don't try to be the lone organizer. Flyer a few blocks, post in local Buy Nothing or Nextdoor groups, and call one quick coffee meeting at a library or coffee shop. You want five to eight people willing to commit a few hours a month. At that meeting, agree on a working name, a shared communication channel (a group text or free Slack), and a one-sentence purpose. Without those, decisions stall.

Week 2: Lock down a site. Walk the neighborhood looking for sunny spots (six-plus hours of direct light is the rough minimum) on land someone can actually grant permission for — a church lawn, a school edge, a vacant city lot, or a willing homeowner's side yard. Contact the owner in writing. Ask specifically about water access, liability, and whether the use can run at least one full growing season. Doing this before buying anything saves the project from collapsing in month two.

Week 3: Materials and money. Estimate small: four to eight raised beds, untreated lumber or cinder blocks, screws, a hose long enough to reach the spigot, basic hand tools, seeds and starts for the current planting window, and bagged compost or a soil-test kit (many county extension offices test cheaply). Funding usually comes from a mix of micro-fundraising, a small local grant, donated lumber from a hardware store, and members chipping in. Don't accept treated lumber as a donation if it might leach.

Week 4: Build and assign maintenance. Pick a Saturday for a build day, supply pizza and water, and finish the beds and a simple kiosk or whiteboard for messages. Before people leave, fill out a maintenance roster: who waters which days, who handles weekend watering, who is the contact for the landowner, and how the group will rotate end-of-season cleanup. Write a one-page rulebook covering shared tools, pet rules, and what happens to unharvested produce.

Two patterns are worth committing to early. First, plan a small visible win in the first growing season — even a handful of beds full of lettuce, radishes, and herbs — because nothing recruits new volunteers like seeing food coming out of the lot. Second, accept that the project will lose a few members to life changes; design roles so any single person can disappear without the garden dying.
